Ezra 1: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, 538 BC, he allows the Jews in Babylon to return and rebuild the temple. Persia had taken Babylon in 539 BC.
Ezra 2: The chapter lists those who returned with Zerubbabel, 42,360 in all (Ezra 2:64), to the Persian province of Judah. The same list appears in Nehemiah 7.
Ezra 3: In the seventh month the returned exiles rebuild the altar, and in the second year they lay the temple's foundation (Ezra 3:1, 8), about 536 BC.
Ezra 4: Opponents stop the building until the reign of Darius. The chapter also includes later letters from the reigns of Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and Artaxerxes in the 5th century BC; Ezra 4:8–6:18 is written in Aramaic.
Ezra 5: In the second year of Darius I, 520 BC, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urge the people to resume building (Ezra 4:24–5:1).
Ezra 6: Cyrus's decree is found at Achmetha (Ecbatana), and the temple is finished on the third of Adar in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15), 515 BC.
Ezra 7: Ezra, a priest and scribe, leaves Babylon in the first month and reaches Jerusalem in the fifth month of Artaxerxes' seventh year (Ezra 7:8–9), 458 BC.
Ezra 8: Ezra's group gathers at the river Ahava and travels about four months to Jerusalem without a military escort (Ezra 8:22).
Ezra 9: Soon after Ezra's arrival in 458 BC, leaders report that many have married women of the surrounding peoples.
Ezra 10: The people gather in Jerusalem on the twentieth day of the ninth month, sitting in the rain (Ezra 10:9), and the matter is settled over three months.
Nehemiah 1: In the month Chisleu of the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, 445 BC, Nehemiah is at Shushan (Susa), a Persian royal city, when he hears that Jerusalem's walls are broken down.
Nehemiah 2: In the month Nisan, Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, receives permission to rebuild Jerusalem and inspects the walls at night.
Nehemiah 3: The chapter lists the groups that repaired each section of Jerusalem's wall and gates.
Nehemiah 4: Sanballat of Samaria and Tobiah the Ammonite threaten the builders, who work with weapons at hand.
Nehemiah 5: Nehemiah, governor of Judah for twelve years (Nehemiah 5:14), stops nobles from charging interest and taking land from poorer Jews.
Nehemiah 6: The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul, in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15), in late summer of 445 BC.
Nehemiah 7: Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers and finds the register of those who first returned, repeated from Ezra 2.
Nehemiah 8: On the first day of the seventh month, Ezra reads the law to the people from a wooden pulpit at the water gate, and they keep the feast of tabernacles.
Nehemiah 9: On the twenty-fourth day of the same month, the people fast, confess, and recount their history.
Nehemiah 10: The leaders, Levites, and priests sign a covenant to keep the law, the sabbath, and the temple offerings.
Nehemiah 11: Lots are cast to bring one in ten of the people to live in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:1).
Nehemiah 12: The chapter lists priests and Levites from Zerubbabel's time onward, then describes the dedication of the wall with two choirs.
Nehemiah 13: Nehemiah returns to Artaxerxes in the king's thirty-second year, 433 BC, then comes back to Jerusalem and corrects abuses (Nehemiah 13:6–7).
Esther 1: In the third year of Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, 486–465 BC), the king holds a feast at Shushan the palace (Esther 1:2–3). His empire runs "from India even unto Ethiopia" (Esther 1:1).
Esther 2: Esther is taken to the king in the tenth month, Tebeth, of his seventh year (Esther 2:16), about 479 BC.
Esther 3: In the twelfth year of Ahasuerus, Haman casts lots (pur) in the first month, Nisan, and they fall on the twelfth month, Adar (Esther 3:7).
Esther 4: Mordecai mourns at the king's gate as the decree reaches every province.
Esther 5: Esther goes before the king uninvited on the third day of her fast and invites him and Haman to a banquet.
Esther 6: On a sleepless night, the king reads the court chronicles and finds that Mordecai once saved his life.
Esther 7: At Esther's second banquet, Haman is exposed and hanged.
Esther 8: On the twenty-third day of the third month, Sivan, a new decree is sent to 127 provinces (Esther 8:9).
Esther 9: On the thirteenth of Adar the Jews defend themselves. The feast of Purim is set on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar.
Esther 10: The book closes with Mordecai second to the king, as recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia" (Esther 10:2).
